lines.text: The Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, July 17, 1981. Two walkways hang above a packed atrium.
At 5 past 7 in the evening, the upper walkway gives way.
It drops onto the walkway below it, and both fall into the crowd below.
It wasn't bad steel or bad workmanship that started it. The federal report says so.
It took a weak detail, a change in how the rods were hung, and a review that let it through.
Here is the hotel, the design, the change, the last minutes, the failure, the findings, and what changed after.
The Hyatt Regency opened in 1980, a new tower hotel in downtown Kansas City.
Its showpiece was a tall atrium, roofed in glass, between the tower and the meeting rooms.
Three walkways crossed it, on the second, third and fourth floors.
They linked the hotel tower to its meeting rooms, high above the lobby floor.
The third floor walkway ran off to one side, on its own rods.
The fourth floor walkway ran directly above the second.
No columns stood under them. They hung from the roof on steel rods.
The fourth floor walkway hung from 6 rods, tied into the roof framing.
That Friday, the hotel held a dance in the atrium.
By early evening, the crowd was estimated at 1,500 to 2,000 people.
Some watched from the walkways. Why did that matter? For that, we need the drawings.
Each walkway rested on steel box beams, laid across underneath its deck.
Each box beam was two 8-inch steel channels, welded toe to toe into a hollow box.
A hanger rod passed down through holes in the beam.
Under the beam sat a washer and a nut. The beam simply rested on them.
In the original design, one long rod ran from the roof, through the fourth floor beam, down to the second.
Each beam had its own nut on that rod, so each carried only its own walkway.
The rod carried both walkways. Each nut held just one.
Sounds solid, doesn't it? Investigators later tested that original connection in a lab.
It would have had only about 60% of the strength the building code expected.
So where was the weak spot? The beam. Its thin edges could bend round the washer and split along the weld.
So the walkways began with less margin than the code required. Then the design changed.
Who decides exactly how each part is made? The steel fabricator, in its shop drawings.
Those drawings used two rods instead of one long one.
One rod hung the fourth floor beam from the roof.
A second rod, set 4 inches inward, hung the second floor beam from the fourth floor beam.
As reported, the fabricator asked the engineers about the change by phone, and it was approved verbally.
The engineering firm later disputed that call.
But the shop drawings came back stamped as reviewed, by the contractor, the engineer and the architect.
As reported, the outside detailer assumed the connection had already been designed, and did no calculations on it.
On paper, a rod had moved a few inches.
So what really changed? In the steel, the weight now took a different path.
The lower walkway no longer hung from the roof. It hung from the upper walkway's beams.
So the nut under each fourth floor beam carried the upper walkway, and the lower one as well.
How much more? Those connections now carried 2 times the load of the original design.
A connection that was already weak now had double the work. And the crowd was coming.
Friday, July 17. People begin arriving for the dance in the afternoon.
Seats fill up, and people start to gather on the walkways to watch.
A television news crew was there, filming the dance.
From that tape, investigators estimated up to 63 people on the second and fourth floor walkways.
Too many people? No. That was far less weight than the walkways were designed to carry.
At 4 past 7, the band returns from its break for a dance contest.
Which connection would go first? Under the fourth floor walkway, any one of them could.
Yet the load on them reached, at most, only 31% of what a connection built to code should hold.
From the day they were built, the report found, the walkways could barely hold their own weight.
How long did it hold? Moments after the band came back, the first connection gave way.
It began at the east end of the fourth floor walkway's middle box beam.
The beam's lower edges bent up around the washer. The weld along the bottom split open.
The rod and its nut pulled straight through the beam.
Its load jumped to the connections beside it. They failed too.
The fourth floor walkway swung down onto the second floor walkway.
Then both fell onto the lobby floor.
The roof rods were left hanging, empty.
At 8 past 7, the fire department took the first call for help.
Rescuers worked through the night to free people trapped beneath the walkways.
113 people died, and 186 were injured.
In loss of life and injuries, the report called it the most devastating structural collapse ever in the United States.
Why did it happen? Days later, federal investigators arrived to find out.
The National Bureau of Standards team reached Kansas City on July 21.
They weighed fallen spans and cut out beams, rods and nuts to study.
The walkways weighed about 8% more than the drawings estimated, a small difference.
In the lab, they built copies of the connection and loaded them until they failed.
Under the code, each fourth floor connection should have held at least 302 kilonewtons.
The tests put them at about 83 kilonewtons on average.
The finding: the connections did not have enough load capacity.
Why so little? Two factors. The original detail was too weak, and the rod change doubled its load.
Bad steel, or bad welding? Neither the workmanship nor the materials started it.
And a twist. With the original rods, the third floor walkway would have been the weakest, at about 53%.
So who was responsible for designing one small connection?
What happened to the engineers? Missouri's licensing board revoked the licences of two of them, for gross negligence and misconduct.
Their professional society, ASCE, answered with a policy in 1985.
The engineer of record is responsible for the whole steel design, connections included.
Under that policy, a connection is never left between the designer and the fabricator.
On the night they fell, the load on those connections was at most 31% of what the code expected them to hold.
A weak detail. A rod moved 4 inches. A review that let it through.
Which link should have been caught first: the detail, the change, or the review? Tell us in the comments.
